name: AI and Cybersecurity Careers
objectives: Given real job posts in your area, describe three entry-level cybersecurity jobs and how AI is changing them, in one sentence each, using the posts

Given security duties from your service, write three cyber skills you already have in civilian words and match them to a NICCS Cyber Career Pathways role, with clearance details listed only as your security office allows
For your target cyber role, find one training path and check on official pages what VA may pay, confirming the program qualifies before you start

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Cyber jobs and how AI is changing them
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name three entry-level cybersecurity jobs and say what each one does day to day.
This lesson builds toward: Given real job posts in your area, you will describe three entry-level cybersecurity jobs and how AI is changing them, in one sentence each, using the posts.
Cybersecurity means protecting computers, networks and information from people who want to steal, change or break them.
Common starting jobs include: security operations center (SOC) analyst, who watches alerts and checks if they are real attacks; IT support with security duties, who sets up accounts and fixes access problems; and governance, risk and compliance (GRC) analyst, who checks that an organization follows its security rules.
AI now helps sort alerts, summarize logs and spot unusual activity. Attackers use AI too, for example to write convincing scam emails. That means employers want people who can use AI tools and still judge what is real.
Words to know:
- SOC: security operations center: the team that watches for and responds to attacks.
- Alert: a warning a security tool raises when it sees something unusual.
- GRC: governance, risk and compliance: making sure an organization follows its security rules and laws.
Try it now: Search a job site for "SOC analyst", "IT support" and "GRC analyst" in your area. For each, write one sentence about what the job does, using the posts.
You can now name three entry-level cyber jobs and explain what each one does.

check.why: Cybersecurity protects computers, networks and information from attacks and mistakes.

check.q: You read three SOC analyst posts. What do you write down?
options: One sentence on what the job does day to day, from the posts
Nothing; posts are all the same
check.why: Describing the daily work from real posts shows you what the job really is.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Translating your service into cyber skills
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write three cyber skills you already have from military service, in civilian words.
This lesson builds toward: Given security duties from your service, you will write three cyber skills you already have in civilian words and match them to a NICCS Cyber Career Pathways role, with clearance details listed only as your security office allows.
You may not have worked in cyber, but you probably practiced its basics. OPSEC (operations security) is protecting information from the enemy. Standing watch is monitoring. Reporting a security incident up the chain is incident response. Controlling who enters a building is access control.
If you held a security clearance, say so on your résumé in the way your security office allows (usually the level and whether it is active). Many cyber employers value it.
The NICCS website from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has a section for veterans and a Cyber Career Pathways Tool that shows cyber roles and the skills each needs. Use it with My Next Move for Veterans to match your job code.
Step by step:
- List three security habits from your service (OPSEC, watch, access control, reporting).
- Ask an AI assistant: "Translate these military security duties into cybersecurity skills employers use."
- Compare with the roles on the NICCS Cyber Career Pathways Tool.
- Keep the three skills that are true and easy to explain.
Words to know:
- OPSEC: operations security: keeping useful information away from an opponent.
- Access control: deciding who is allowed into a place, system or file.
- Incident response: what a team does when something bad or suspicious happens.
- NICCS: National Initiative for Cybersecurity Careers and Studies, CISA's cyber career and training website.
Official sources:
- NICCS, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency
- My Next Move for Veterans (U.S. Department of Labor)
Try it now: Write three security duties from your own service. Ask an AI assistant to put them in cyber words, then check them against one role in the NICCS Cyber Career Pathways Tool.
You can now describe your military security experience as cyber skills an employer recognizes.

check.q: Standing watch in the military is most like which cyber task?
check.why: Watching for anything unusual and reporting it is what cyber monitoring does.

check.q: You want to put your clearance on a résumé. What do you do?
options: Describe the classified programs you worked on
Leave out all of your service
List it only the way your security office allows, usually level and status
Ask the AI to guess how to list it
check.why: Clearances are listed only as the security office allows, never with classified details.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Finding official training and help paying for it
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find one training path and check on official pages what VA may pay.
This lesson builds toward: For your target cyber role, you will find one training path and check on official pages what VA may pay, confirming the program qualifies before you start.
NICCS has an Education and Training Catalog where you can search cyber courses. Job posts will tell you which entry certification employers want; CompTIA Security+ is one that appears often in entry-level posts, but read posts in your own area.
VA can repay licensing and certification test fees if you have a qualifying GI Bill benefit. When we checked va.gov in October 2026, the limit was no more than $2,000 per test, and it uses some of your entitlement. VA's VET TEC 2.0 program funds non-degree high-tech training such as computer programming, software and information sciences, with a limited number of places each year. The VET TEC page did not list cybersecurity by name, so check whether a program qualifies.
The Department of Labor's Veterans' Employment and Training Service (VETS) runs the Transition Assistance Program and points veterans to employment help and apprenticeships.
Step by step:
- Search the NICCS Education and Training Catalog for an entry course.
- Check five job posts for the most-requested certification.
- Read the va.gov test fee page and the VET TEC 2.0 page.
- Check dol.gov/agencies/vets for job help and apprenticeships.
Words to know:
- Entry-level: a job for people starting out in a field.
- Apprenticeship: a paid job where you learn on the job while you work.
Official sources:
- VA: Licensing and certification test fees
- VA: VET TEC 2.0
- U.S. Department of Labor, Veterans' Employment and Training Service
- NICCS, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency
Try it now: Find one entry cyber course in the NICCS catalog and the certification most asked for in local job posts. Then open the va.gov test fee page and note whether your benefit qualifies.
You can now find an official cyber training path and check what VA may help pay for.

options: A free cyber training and career site run by CISA
check.why: NICCS is CISA's site with a training catalog and career pathways tool.

check.q: You found a cyber course you like. What do you check before counting on VA to pay?
options: Whether the program qualifies, on the official va.gov page
check.why: Eligibility and program lists change, so you confirm on va.gov before you start.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Using AI as a security study partner
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to learn one security idea and explain it back in your own words.
This lesson builds toward: Given one security idea such as the CIA triad, you will use an AI assistant to learn the idea and explain it back in your own words, using only made-up examples, with the AI confirming your explanation.
A key idea in security is the CIA triad: confidentiality (only the right people see information), integrity (information is not changed without permission) and availability (systems work when people need them).
Ask an AI assistant to explain one idea with a military example, then explain it back in your own words and ask the AI to check you. This "teach-back" is how you know you really understand.
Never paste passwords, real company logs, customer data or anything from a work system into a public AI tool. Use made-up or cleaned examples. Many employers have rules about which AI tools are allowed.
Step by step:
- Pick one idea, such as the CIA triad.
- Ask: "Explain this in simple words with a military example."
- Explain it back in your own words.
- Ask the AI: "Is my explanation right? What did I miss?"
- Use only made-up examples, never real data.
Words to know:
- CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three goals of security.
- Teach-back: explaining something back in your own words to prove you understand it.
- Log: a computer's record of what happened and when.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to explain the CIA triad using a military example. Then write your own two-sentence explanation and ask it to check you.
You can now use AI to learn a security idea and prove you understand it with a teach-back.

check.q: In the CIA triad, what does confidentiality mean?
options: Only the right people can see the information
check.why: Confidentiality means information is seen only by people allowed to see it.

check.q: You want to practice a security idea with AI. Which example do you use?
options: A real log from your job
check.why: Made-up examples let you practice without sharing real company or personal information.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking a suspicious email
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the warning signs in a suspicious email and decide what to do, without clicking anything.
This lesson builds toward: Given a suspicious email, you will list its warning signs and choose a safe response, without clicking anything and with private details replaced by placeholders before using AI.
Phishing is a fake message that tries to make you click a link, open a file, or give up a password or money. Checking reported emails is a common first task for junior analysts.
Warning signs: the sender's address does not match the company, the message rushes or threatens you, it asks for a password, code, payment or gift cards, the link text and real address are different, or there is an unexpected attachment.
To use AI safely, copy only the text of the message, and replace names, email addresses and account numbers with placeholders like [name]. Ask the AI to list warning signs. Do not click links or open attachments. Hover over a link (on a computer) to see its real address.
Step by step:
- Do not click links or open attachments.
- Look at the sender's real address and the link addresses.
- Copy only the message text and replace private details with placeholders.
- Ask an AI assistant: "List the phishing warning signs in this email."
- Decide: report it, delete it, or confirm with the company using a number you know is real.
Words to know:
- Phishing: a fake message that tries to trick you into clicking, sharing a password or sending money.
- Attachment: a file sent with an email.
- Placeholder: a stand-in like [name] used instead of real private details.
Try it now: Find a suspicious email in your spam folder (or ask an AI to write a made-up one). Without clicking anything, list its warning signs yourself, then ask the AI and compare lists.
You can now spot the warning signs of a phishing email and check it safely with AI help.

options: A safe way to share files
A fake message that tricks you into clicking or sharing
check.why: Phishing messages pretend to be real to get you to click or share information.

check.q: An email says "Your account is locked, click here now". What is your safe first step?
options: Click to see if it is real
Do not click; check the sender and hover to see the real address
check.why: You check without clicking: the sender, the real link address and the pressure to act fast.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing an incident note and telling your story
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a five-line incident note and two résumé lines that connect your service to cyber work.
This lesson builds toward: For the email you checked and your service, you will write a five-line incident note and two résumé lines that connect your service to cyber work, short, clear and factual, ending with what you recommend.
Analysts write short notes so others can act. A simple five-line incident note covers: what arrived, the warning signs, the risk, what you did, and what you recommend. It is like a SALUTE or spot report: clear, short and factual.
Your résumé should connect your service to cyber work with action and results, for example: "Enforced OPSEC and access control for a 120-person unit; completed [course] in network security, 2026."
Use AI to tighten your wording, but every line must be true. In interviews, tell one short story about a time you noticed something wrong and reported it.
Step by step:
- Write the five lines: what arrived, warning signs, risk, action, recommendation.
- Keep each line short and factual.
- Write two résumé lines linking your service to cyber skills.
- Ask an AI assistant to make them clearer, then check every word is true.
Words to know:
- Incident note: a short written report of a security event and what was done.
- Recommendation: what you suggest should happen next.
Try it now: Final task: write the five-line incident note for the email you checked in Lesson 5, then write two résumé lines that connect your military experience to a cyber job.
You can now check a suspicious email like a junior analyst, report it clearly, and present your service as cyber experience.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Warning signs found Fewer than three warning signs, or the learner clicked the link. At least three warning signs listed without clicking anything. The learner found a sign the AI missed, or the AI found one they missed, and they can explain it. Safe use of AI Real names, emails or numbers were pasted into the AI. Private details were replaced with placeholders, or a made-up example was used. The learner explains which details they removed and why. Incident note Missing lines, or opinions instead of facts. Five short, factual lines: what arrived, warning signs, risk, what you did, what you recommend. The recommendation names a clear next step for the team, such as reporting or blocking the sender. Résumé lines Lines are vague or include classified details. Two lines that connect a real military security duty to a cyber job in civilian words. The lines use words from a NICCS pathway role or real job posts. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does a five-line incident note end with?
check.why: The note ends with your recommendation so a reader knows what to do next.

check.q: Which résumé line connects service to cyber work best?
options: "Enforced access control for a 90-person unit; completed a network security course, 2026"
"Have a clearance; ask me about missions"
check.why: It shows a real security duty, a size and training, in civilian words.
